name: Gibson & Kalamazoo
description: Gibson/Kalamazoo combo organ listing copy — the G-101, K-101, and G-201, per the Combo Organ Service page listing these as models CEPCo specializes in. Historical/technical details sourced from Wikipedia and cross-referenced combo organ references; anything not confidently verifiable was left out rather than guessed.

nodes.label: Kalamazoo K-101
nodes.copy:
Every Gibson and Kalamazoo combo organ we restore for sale goes through the same meticulous process we're known for, with dozens of hours devoted to bringing each instrument to exceptional playing condition. We prioritize period-correct vintage components whenever possible, and turn to the best available reproduction parts when originals are no longer viable — always working to preserve the instrument's original character and tone. The result is an organ that plays and sounds better than it likely has in decades.

This organ was first sold in 1966 as the Kalamazoo K-101, using the budget "Kalamazoo" name Gibson applied to its entry-level gear. Electronically and mechanically it's identical to the Gibson G-101 that followed — the only meaningful change between badges was the addition of a cast Gibson logo to the front panel. Built by the Lowrey Organ Company for Gibson's parent company, Chicago Musical Instruments, it's a 61-key, five-octave single-manual organ with 16', 8', 4' and 2-2/3' footages across reed, string and flute voices, plus a foldback bass section and a mixture tab combining the 4' and 2-2/3' tones.

nodes.label: Gibson G-101
nodes.copy:
Every Gibson and Kalamazoo combo organ we restore for sale goes through the same meticulous process we're known for, with dozens of hours devoted to bringing each instrument to exceptional playing condition. We prioritize period-correct vintage components whenever possible, and turn to the best available reproduction parts when originals are no longer viable — always working to preserve the instrument's original character and tone. The result is an organ that plays and sounds better than it likely has in decades.

Introduced in 1966 as the rebadged successor to the Kalamazoo K-101 — Gibson swapped in its own logo shortly after launch to boost sales, but the electronics and mechanics carried over unchanged. Built by the Lowrey Organ Company for Gibson's parent company, Chicago Musical Instruments, it's a 61-key, five-octave single-manual organ with 16', 8', 4' and 2-2/3' footages across reed, string and flute voices, plus a foldback bass section and a mixture tab combining the 4' and 2-2/3' tones. It's best known today as the organ Ray Manzarek played with The Doors — often mistaken in accounts of the band for a Farfisa or Vox.

nodes.label: Gibson G-201
nodes.copy:
Every Gibson and Kalamazoo combo organ we restore for sale goes through the same meticulous process we're known for, with dozens of hours devoted to bringing each instrument to exceptional playing condition. We prioritize period-correct vintage components whenever possible, and turn to the best available reproduction parts when originals are no longer viable — always working to preserve the instrument's original character and tone. The result is an organ that plays and sounds better than it likely has in decades.

The G-201 pairs the same core electronics as the G-101 with a two-manual spinet-style layout, trading the G-101's foldback bass section and mixture tab for a second, shorter keyboard and an added "Manual Attack" tab.
